claims.claim: The microfluidic chips are composed of two stacked PDMS layers.
claims.source: We fabricated microfluidic chips that are composed of two stacked PDMS layers (see Figure 1a–c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 to Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The bottom layer had rectangular chambers with height of ∼2.4 µm and lateral dimensions ranging from 10 × 10 µm to 60 × 80 µm.
claims.source: The bottom layer had structures of three different heights: (i) Rectangular chambers with height of ∼2.4 µm and lateral dimensions ranging from 10 × 10 µm to 60 × 80 µm (blue part in Figure 1b)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The bottom layer had reservoir channels with height of ∼30 µm and width of 100 µm.
claims.source: (ii) Reservoir channels with height of ∼30 µm and width of 100 µm (red part in Figure 1b)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The bottom layer had thin connector channels with height of ∼0.9 µm and width of ∼0.9 µm that connect the reservoirs and chambers.
claims.source: (iii) thin connectors channels with height of ∼0.9 µm and width of ∼0.9 µm (green part in Figure 1c) that connect the reservoirs and the chambers.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The upper layer of the device consisted of air-filled PDMS channels that served as pneumatic pressure valves.
claims.source: The upper layer of the device consisted of air-filled PDMS channels that were aligned directly above the reservoir channels and connected to a high-pressure argon line thus serving as pneumatic pressure valves (Unger et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to the valve technology.

claims.claim: Upon increasing the pressure of the air-filled channels, the ceiling of the lower layer deflected downward and closed the entrance to the connector lines.
claims.source: Upon increasing the pressure of the air-filled channels in the upper layer, the ceiling of the lower layer (thickness ∼20 µm) deflected downward above the reservoir channels and closed the entrance to the connector lines.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of valve operation.

claims.claim: The design allowed spatial isolation of the central PDMS chambers from the rest of the chip to obtain totally isolated 3D confined volumes.
claims.source: Using this design, we were able to spatially isolate the central PDMS chambers (blue in Figure 1b) from the rest of the chip and to obtain totally isolated 3D confined volumes for studying the Min patterns.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the experimental design.

claims.claim: A continuous SLB was formed on all the inner walls of the chambers after flushing with SUVs and incubating for ∼1 hr.
claims.source: After the device was flushed with SUVs and incubated for ∼1 hr, a nice continuous SLB was formed on all the inner walls of the chambers (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claims.claim: The feature of microchambers covered by an SLB from all sides distinguishes this approach from previous studies that reconstituted Min proteins in fabricated structures.
claims.source: This feature of our microchambers that are covered by an SLB from all sides is what distinguishes our approach from previous studies that reconstituted Min proteins in fabricated structures (Loose et al., 2008; Ivanov and Mizuuchi, 2010; Schweizer et al., 2012; Martos et al., 2015; Zieske and Schwille, 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014; Zieske and Schwille, 2014; Vecchiarelli et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key distinguishing feature with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Upon closing the pressure valves, truly confined chambers were obtained in the microfluidic devices.
claims.source: These results corroborated that upon closing the pressure valves, we obtained truly confined chambers in our microfluidic devices.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from quality control experiments.

claims.claim: In most cases, the Min proteins showed a defined pattern in each chamber that was stable for the duration of movie acquisition (∼10 min).
claims.source: In most of the cases, the Min proteins showed a defined pattern in each chamber that was stable for the duration of the movie acquisition (∼10 min).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claims.claim: The typical time to reestablish the Min zone in the microchambers was 1−5 min.
claims.source: As can be seen from Figure 1d–f, the typical time it took to reestablish the Min zone in these microchambers was 1−5 min.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in the figures.

claims.claim: The large majority of observed patterns (>95%) could be readily classified into oscillations, traveling waves, or rotations.
claims.source: The large majority of observed patterns (>95%) could be readily classified in these three categories.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claims.claim: Clear relations exist between the geometry of the chamber and the observed dynamical Min behavior.
claims.source: As can be seen, clear relations exist between the geometry of the chamber and the observed dynamical Min behavior.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Rotational patterns appear as the majority for chambers with small aspect ratio.
claims.source: (i) Rotational patterns appear as the majority for chambers with small aspect ratio (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: As the chamber aspect ratio increases, the probability to obtain rotational behavior decreases.
claims.source: As the chamber aspect ratio increases, the probability to obtain rotational behavior decreases
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: For chambers with an aspect ratio larger than 2.8, rotational behavior was hardly observed.
claims.source: and for chambers with an aspect ratio larger than 2.8, we hardly observed rotational behavior in our chambers.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Oscillatory behavior predominantly appears when the chamber width is small (∼10 µm).
claims.source: (ii) Oscillatory behavior predominantly appears when the chamber width is small (∼10 µm) (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Traveling waves mainly appear if the chamber length is relatively large.
claims.source: (iii) Traveling waves mainly appear if the chamber length is relatively large (Figure 3c)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: The prevalence of traveling waves increases as the chamber length increases.
claims.source: and their prevalence increases as the chamber length increases.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: If the chamber area is relatively large, the prevalence of obtaining traveling waves increases.
claims.source: Similarly, if the chamber area is relatively large the prevalence of obtaining a traveling waves increases (see. Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: For large chamber areas, the confined chambers reflect the surface waves that were observed on unbound SLBs.
claims.source: For these large areas, the confined chambers reflect the surface waves that were observed on unbound SLBs (Loose et al., 2008; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The clear relation between chamber geometry and dynamical Min patterns unambiguously proves that confinement sets the rules for Min pattern formation.
claims.source: The clear relation found between the chamber geometry and the dynamical Min patterns unambiguously proves that confinement sets the rules for Min pattern formation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The existence of connector lines in the setup adds only second-order effects.
claims.source: It also supports the notion that the existence of the connector lines in our setup adds only second-order effects.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the clear geometry-pattern relationship.

claims.claim: By using soft fabricated valves, geometrical selection rules of the Min system in truly confined 3D structures in vitro were extracted and studied for the first time.
claims.source: Thus, by using the soft fabricated valves, we were able to extract and study, for the first time, the geometrical selection rules of the Min system in truly confined 3D structures in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key achievement of the study.

claims.claim: The phase diagram is nicely separated into three different regions: rotations, oscillations in narrow chambers, and traveling waves in large and long chambers.
claims.source: As can be seen from Figure 4a, the phase diagram is nicely separated into three different regions: (i) The majority pattern is rotations; (ii) oscillations are the most prevalent pattern in narrow chambers, in line with previous observation in semi-3D-confined structures (Zieske and Schwille, 2013, 2014); and (iii) as expected (Loose et al., 2008, 2011a), the most prevalent behavior for large and long chambers is that of traveling waves.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4a with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In fully confined 3D chambers, a large part of the phase diagram is occupied by rotational behavior.
claims.source: The most striking, and unexpected, result of this study is that in fully confined 3D chambers, a large part of the phase diagram is occupied by rotational behavior, i.e., Min patterns that rotate around a fixed point in a spiral fashion.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the phase diagram.

claims.claim: When chambers become too narrow, rotational centers are less stable and oscillations are formed.
claims.source: When the chambers becomes too narrow, these rotational centers are less stable, presumably due to reflection of the Min concentration front from the chamber boundaries, and oscillations are formed.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the phase diagram data.

claims.claim: Oscillations appear to be a derivative phenomenon that results from destabilization of spiral rotating patterns by the chamber walls.
claims.source: Oscillations thus appear to be a derivative phenomenon that results from destabilization of spiral rotating patterns by the chamber walls.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the phase diagram data.

claims.claim: For very large areas, the interaction between multiple rotational centers equilibrates such that the stable behavior becomes a traveling wave.
claims.source: In the other extreme, for very large areas, the interaction between multiple rotational centers will equilibrate in such a way that the stable behavior becomes a traveling wave.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the phase diagram data.

claims.claim: The actual concentration of Min proteins in the chambers was significantly (∼factor 5) higher than the injected stock solution value.
claims.source: As can be seen (Figure 5a), the actual concentration of the Min proteins in our chambers was significantly (∼factor 5 higher than the value for the injected stock solution.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a based on GFP calibration measurements.

claims.claim: A wide distribution of Min protein concentrations was observed in the chambers, particularly for MinE.
claims.source: Furthermore, a wide distribution is observed, particularly for MinE.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the concentration measurements shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: No relation was observed between chamber size and the measured concentration of Min proteins.
claims.source: Note that we did not observe a relation between the chamber size and the measured concentration of the Min proteins.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the concentration measurements.

claims.claim: The concentration of MinD in the chambers was 4.5 ± 0.5 µM (mean ± SD).
claims.source: From these measurements we concluded that the concentration of MinD in our chambers was 4.5 ± 0.5 µM (mean ± SD)
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GFP calibration measurements.

claims.claim: The concentration of MinE in the chambers was 6 ± 3 µM.
claims.source: the concentration of MinE 6 ± 3 µM
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GFP calibration measurements.

claims.claim: The average ratio of [MinE]/[MinD] in the chambers was 1.3 ± 0.5.
claims.source: and the average ratio of [MinE]/[MinD] amounted to 1.3 ± 0.5.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GFP calibration measurements.

claims.claim: The wavelength of Min waves in confined chambers at room temperature was 43 ± 6 µM.
claims.source: We measured a wavelength of 43 ± 6 µM at room temperature.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The wavelength on 2D flat SLBs at room temperature was 78 ± 12 µM.
claims.source: This value is significantly lower than the wavelength of 78 ± 12 µM (n = 30 for traveling waves that we measured on 2D flat SLBs using the exact same protein and lipid composition of the SLB as was used in our microchambers experiments.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: 3D full confinement of the Min system has a clear effect on the characteristic length scale of the system.
claims.source: This shows that the 3D full confinement of the Min system has a clear effect not only on the geometry-selection properties, but also on the characteristic length scale of the system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing wavelengths in 3D chambers versus 2D surfaces.

claims.claim: The velocity of Min patterns in chambers at room temperature was 0.3 ± 0.1 µm/s.
claims.source: inside the chambers we obtained a propagation velocity of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm/s
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: The velocity of Min waves on flat SLB surfaces at room temperature was 0.6 ± 0.2 µm/s.
claims.source: While on flat SLB surfaces we measured v = 0.6 ± 0.2 µm/s, similar to previous measured values (Loose et al., 2011a)
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The reduced wavelength inside the chambers was accompanied by a reduced velocity.
claims.source: The reduced wavelength inside the chambers was thus accompanied with a reduced velocity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing wavelengths and velocities.

claims.claim: The measured viscosity of the crowding solution (4% PEG 8000, 4% Ficol 400, 4% BSA) is 9.9 ± 0.05 cP.
claims.source: The measured viscosity of this solution is 9.9 ± 0.05 cP, i.e., one order of magnitude larger than that of water.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result.

claims.claim: The viscosity of the crowding solution is close to the estimated viscosity inside E. coli cells.
claims.source: Though the exact viscosity inside E. coli cells is unknown, this value is close to the estimated one (Trovato and Tozzini, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Increasing the viscosity of the environment resulted in a factor 2 reduction of the wavelength from 43 ± 6 µm to 23 ± 4 µm.
claims.source: Increasing the viscosity of the environment resulted in a factor 2 reduction of the wavelength from 43 ± 6 µm to 23 ± 4 µm.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The reduction in wavelength with increased viscosity is comparable to the reduction observed by Martos et al. in the presence of 140 g/l Ficol.
claims.source: This reduction in the wavelength is comparable to the reduction in wavelength that was observed by Martos et al. in the presence of 140 g/l Ficol (Martos et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work with citation.

claims.claim: A very large decrease of more than one order of magnitude in wave velocity was observed with increased viscosity, from 0.3 ± 0.1 µm to 0.02 ± 0.014 µm/s.
claims.source: Next to the reduction in the wavelength, we observed a very large decrease, of more than one order of magnitude, in the wave velocity from 0.3 ± 0.1 µm to 0.02 ± 0.014 µm/s.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: The substantial decrease in velocity with increased viscosity is much larger than what was observed by Martos et al. and is probably related to the different constellations of 2D surfaces versus 3D confined microchambers.
claims.source: Note that this substantial decrease in the velocity is much larger than what was observed by Martos et al. and is probably related to the different constellations of 2D surfaces (used by Martos et al.) in comparison to 3D confined microchambers (in this work).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation comparing to previous work with citation.

claims.claim: The geometry selection properties of the Min system at 37°C are very similar to those observed at room temperature.
claims.source: As can be seen in Figure 3d–f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, the geometry selection properties of the Min system at the elevated temperature of 37°C are very similar to those that were observed at room temperature (n = 198)
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3d-f.

claims.claim: At low aspect ratio of chambers, the prevalence to obtain rotational patterns is high at 37°C and decreases as aspect ratio increases.
claims.source: (i) at low aspect ratio of the chambers (L/W), the prevalence to obtain rotational patterns is high while it decreases as the aspect ratio increases
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data at 37°C.

claims.claim: Oscillatory behavior is observed mainly for narrow chambers at 37°C.
claims.source: (ii) oscillatory behavior is observed mainly for narrow chambers
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data at 37°C.

claims.claim: Traveling waves become dominant for long and large chambers at 37°C.
claims.source: (iii) traveling waves become dominant for long and large chambers.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data at 37°C.

claims.claim: The wavelength at 37°C shows only a small decrease relative to room temperature, from 43 ± 6 µm to 37 ± 9 µm.
claims.source: The wavelength at the elevated temperature (see Figure 6a, n = 34), shows only a small decrease relative to the wavelength at room temperature, that is from 43 ± 6 µm to 37 ± 9 µm (two sample t-test with different variance = 0.001 at β = 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a with statistical test.

claims.claim: For waves on flat 2D SLB surfaces, the wavelength reduced from 78 ± 12 at room temperature to 48 ± 6 µm at 37°C.
claims.source: This contrasts the behavior of waves on flat 2D SLBs surfaces, for which we observed a much more profound effect (Figure 6a, n = 27). In this case the wavelength reduced from 78 ± 12 at room temperature to 48 ± 6 µm at 37°C.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: In confined chambers, confinement is the major cause of reduced wavelength, with elevated temperature adding only a small further reduction.
claims.source: These data thus show that, in confined chambers, confinement is the major cause of the reduced wavelength, with the elevated temperature adding only a small further reduction in the characteristic spatial scale of the system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing wavelength data at different temperatures and confinement conditions.

claims.claim: At T = 37°C, the velocity of Min patterns in chambers was v = 0.5 ± 0.3 µm/s.
claims.source: At T = 37°C, the velocity v = 0.5 ± 0.3 µm/s (velocity for waves only v = 0.5 ± 0.1 µm/s n = 34).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: At T = 37°C, the velocity of waves on flat SLBs was v = 1.4 µm/s.
claims.source: This compares to v = 1.4 µm/s (Figure 6b) for waves propagating on flat SLBs surfaces.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: Similar to conditions in vivo, elevated temperature increases the velocity of Min propagation in vitro, doubling from 23°C to 37°C both on 2D surfaces and in 3D confinement.
claims.source: Thus, similar to the conditions in vivo, where the period of the oscillations is inversely correlated with the temperature (Touhami et al., 2006), elevated temperature increases the velocity of the Min propagation in vitro, doubling from 23°C to 37°C both on 2D surfaces and in 3D confinement.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from velocity measurements with citation to in vivo work.

claims.claim: In contrast to in vivo behavior, the in vitro wavelength is temperature dependent.
claims.source: However, in contrast to the in vivo behavior, the in vitro wavelength is also temperature dependent.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from wavelength measurements comparing to in vivo observations.

claims.claim: The viscosity of the bulk media changes only by a factor of 1.3 from 23°C to 37°C.
claims.source: Since the viscosity of the bulk media change only by a factor of 1.3 from 23°C to 37°C
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known physical property.

claims.claim: The temperature effect on wavelength must be attributed to a change in one of the reaction parameters of the reaction-diffusion Min system.
claims.source: we have to attribute these results to a change in one of the reaction parameters of the reaction-diffusion Min system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: There are different ways to modulate the different dynamical characteristics (wavelength and velocity) of the Min system.
claims.source: We can conclude that there are different ways to modulate the different dynamical characteristics (wavelength and velocity) of the Min system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Total confinement of the Min system within 3D chambers leads to three main types of patterns: rotational patterns in the form of spiral waves (majority), periodic oscillations (mainly if chamber width is small), and traveling waves (mainly if one dimension is larger than typical spatial length scale).
claims.source: In this article, we have shown that total confinement of the Min system within 3D chambers leads to three main type of patterns: (i) rotational patterns in the form of spiral waves, which are the majority of the patterns found; (ii) periodic oscillations that occur mainly if the chamber width is small in comparison to the typical spatial length scale of the system in vitro; (iii) traveling waves that occur mainly if one of the dimensions of the chamber is larger than the typical spatial length scale of the system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: In microchambers, rotational behavior in the form of spiral waves contributes the largest fraction of the phase diagram.
claims.source: In our microchambers, rotational behavior in the form of one or multiple adjacent spiral waves thus contributes the largest fraction of the phase diagram.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the phase diagram.

claims.claim: Spiral waves are common in various biological and chemical reaction-diffusion processes such as Dictyostelium discoideum aggregation, calcium variations in Xenopus laevis oocytes, and the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction.
claims.source: Spiral waves are common in various biological and chemical reaction-diffusion processes such as Dictyostelium discoideum aggregation, calcium variations in Xenopus laevis oocytes, and the famous Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction (see Epstein and Pojman, 1998 and references therein).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claims.claim: Spiral waves were observed for the Min system on flat SLBs.
claims.source: They were also observed for the Min system on flat SLBs (Loose et al., 2008; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: For the BZ reaction, spiral waves were attributed to a Hopf bifurcation mechanism.
claims.source: For example, for the BZ reaction, spiral waves were attributed to a Hopf bifurcation mechanism (Hagan, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: In nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, several symmetry-breaking mechanisms may coexist in different parts of the parameter phase space, resulting in a plethora of static or dynamic patterns.
claims.source: In addition, it is well known that in nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, several symmetry-breaking-mechanisms may coexist in different parts of the parameter phase space and, as result, a plethora of static or dynamic patterns can emerge (Yang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claims.claim: It is possible that in vitro Min patterns emanate from a different symmetry-breaking mechanism than Min oscillations in live cells despite the proteins being the same.
claims.source: In light of this knowledge, it is well possible that in vitro Min patterns, in fact, emanate from a somehow different symmetry-breaking-mechanism than the Min oscillations in live cells despite the fact that the proteins are the same and the patterns share various similar characteristics with the in vivo case.
claims.evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observations.

claims.claim: The existence of spirals in vitro and their abundance in confined microchambers, compared to their absence in vivo where pole-to-pole oscillations dominate, may be related to different symmetry-breaking mechanisms.
claims.source: The existence of spirals in vitro and their abundance in our confined microchambers, when compared to their absence from in vivo observations where pole-to-pole oscillations dominate (Wu et al., 2015), may be related to this.
claims.evidence: This is stated as speculation with citation to in vivo work.

claims.claim: Spiral patterns were not stable in narrow chambers smaller than or equal to the characteristic 10 µm length scale of spirals.
claims.source: We observed that the spiral patterns were found not to be stable in narrow chambers that are smaller than, or equal to, the characteristic 10 µm length scale of spirals.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Pole-to-pole oscillations are established as the chamber walls restrict spirals to form.
claims.source: We observed that pole-to-pole oscillations are established as the chamber walls restrict spirals to form.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: In vitro oscillations appear to be a form of truncated spirals.
claims.source: In other words, in vitro oscillations in fact appear to be a form of truncated spirals.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observations.

claims.claim: The data are the first to suggest that in vitro oscillations are truncated spirals.
claims.source: These data are the first to suggest that in vitro oscillations are truncated spirals
claims.evidence: This is stated as a novel interpretation.

claims.claim: In vivo, spiral rotations were not observed.
claims.source: Please note also that in vivo, spiral rotations were not observed (Wu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous in vivo work.

claims.claim: Spiral rotations were not suggested as the origin of the symmetry-breaking mechanism in theoretical works.
claims.source: Neither were they suggested as the origin of the symmetry-breaking mechanism in theoretical works.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation about the theoretical literature.

claims.claim: In vivo, pole-to-pole oscillations amount to the establishment of a polar zone that is replaced by a second polar zone near the opposite pole within a short time scale.
claims.source: In vivo, the pole-to-pole oscillations amount to the establishment of polar zone that is replaced by a second polar zone near the opposite pole within a short time scale.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a description of in vivo behavior.

claims.claim: In vitro oscillations are more akin to a traveling wave that propagates toward one pole, then is replaced by a wave established near the chamber middle that propagates toward the opposite pole.
claims.source: In contrast to this, in vitro oscillations are more akin to a traveling wave that propagates toward one pole, whereupon it is then replaced by a wave that is established close to the chamber middle and propagates toward the opposite pole
claims.evidence: This is stated as a description of in vitro behavior observed in this study.

claims.claim: Similar oscillation behavior to in vitro was observed in other reconstitution work.
claims.source: Similar behavior was also observed in in vitro oscillations of other reconstitution work (Zieske and Schwille, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The difference in oscillation character between in vivo and in vitro may be the reason why steep in vitro Min gradients that would restrict FtsZ localization to a single ring could not be established.
claims.source: This may also be the reason why steep in vitro Min gradients that would restrict FtsZ localization to a single ring could not have been established.
claims.evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observations.

claims.claim: In vivo traveling waves represent a form of abnormal behavior which occurs if MinE function is impaired or in other anomalous cases.
claims.source: Note that in all these cases, the in vivo traveling waves represent a form of abnormal behavior which occurs if the MinE function is impaired or in other anomalous cases.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of in vivo observations.

claims.claim: In vitro, traveling waves can be a generic feature of the Min system.
claims.source: This contrasts to the in vitro case, where traveling waves can be a generic feature of the Min system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from in vitro observations.

claims.claim: On flat 2D SLBs, spiral waves are not confined and waves from one center can travel long distances and interfere with waves from a second spiral center to form traveling waves.
claims.source: First, on flat 2D SLBs the spirals waves are not confined and hence waves that emanate from one center can travel long distance and interfere with waves that emanate from a second spiral center to form traveling waves.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an explanation for traveling wave formation on 2D surfaces.

claims.claim: In large chambers, the intrinsic Min pattern formation mechanism and reflection from chamber walls result in annihilation of spiral centers and establishment of traveling waves.
claims.source: In our chambers, when their area became large, the intrinsic Min pattern formation mechanism and the reflection from the chambers walls resulted in the annihilation of spiral centers and the establishment of traveling waves, similar to the 2D case where boundaries are absent.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an explanation for traveling wave formation in large chambers.

claims.claim: Due to the small surface-to-volume ratio in typical in vitro assays, the actual concentration of proteins on the membrane and the replenished reservoir is higher than in vivo.
claims.source: However, due to the small surface-to-volume ratio in typical in vitro assays, the actual concentration of the proteins on the membrane and the replenished reservoir of new Min proteins is higher than in vivo (cf. the above section on Min concentration in the microchambers).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an explanation with reference to the concentration measurements.

claims.claim: The high protein concentration situation in vitro is qualitatively different from in vivo where cytosolic concentration drops to a low value during polar zone or Min band formation.
claims.source: This situation is qualitatively different from the in vivo case where, during the formation of polar zone or a Min band, most of the MinD proteins are recruited to the membrane and the cytosolic concentration thus drops to a low value.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison between in vitro and in vivo conditions.

claims.claim: Vecchiarelli et al. suggested that in vitro spiral waves are related to high concentration of Min proteins, while reconstituting under limiting concentration conditions resulted in Min bursts reminiscent of behavior in cells.
claims.source: Indeed, in a very recent publication, Vecchiarelli et al. suggested that in vitro spirals waves are related to high concentration of the Min proteins, while reconstituting the Min system under limiting concentration conditions resulted in a dynamical series of Min bursts that are reminiscent of the behavior in cells (Vecchiarelli et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claims.claim: When MinE was replaced by membrane-binding deficient mutant MinE11–88, Min waves were supported at high protein concentration but bursting dynamics were absent.

results.result: The authors developed a novel microfluidic system consisting of two-layer PDMS chips with fully confined 3D chambers (2.4 μm height, 10×10 to 60×80 μm lateral dimensions) that are lipid-bilayer coated on all surfaces and can be isolated using pneumatic pressure valves. This represents the first in vitro study of the Min system in fully confined, lithography-defined, 3D chambers with complete SLB coverage.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 provide detailed technical specifications and validation of the microfluidic device design. The novelty claim (C1, C71) is supported by the unique combination of features: full 3D confinement, complete SLB coating on all chamber walls, and valve-based isolation. Quality control experiments (C72) confirmed true confinement. This is a well-documented methodological advance over previous semi-confined systems.

results.result: Three distinct dynamical behaviors of Min proteins were identified in confined chambers: pole-to-pole oscillations (predominantly in narrow ~10 μm chambers), spiral rotations (majority pattern in chambers with small aspect ratio <2.8), and traveling waves (in large/long chambers). Clear geometric selection rules were established showing that chamber geometry determines Min pattern formation, with confinement being the primary determinant.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C87 document systematic observations across 553 chambers with >95% classification success (C75). The geometric relationships are well-characterized with specific quantitative thresholds (e.g., aspect ratio >2.8 for rotation suppression, C79). Statistical support is provided through extensive sampling across chamber geometries. The conclusion that confinement sets pattern formation rules (C85) is well-justified by the clear geometry-pattern correlations.

results.result: Spiral rotations constitute the dominant Min pattern in fully confined 3D chambers, occupying the largest fraction of the geometrical phase diagram. This finding was unexpected and represents a major departure from previous in vitro studies on 2D surfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 and C126 consistently report spiral rotations as the majority pattern, supported by the phase diagram data (Figure 4). The characterization as 'striking and unexpected' (C89) is justified given that previous 2D studies primarily observed traveling waves. The quantitative phase diagram provides clear visual evidence for this dominance across a wide range of chamber geometries.

results.result: In vitro oscillations appear to be truncated spirals that form when chamber walls destabilize rotational centers in narrow chambers (≤10 μm characteristic length scale). This represents the first suggestion that oscillations are a derivative phenomenon resulting from geometric constraints on spiral patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 and C133-C136 present a coherent mechanistic interpretation supported by observations across the phase diagram. The transition from spirals to oscillations in narrow chambers is documented, and the interpretation as 'truncated spirals' (C135) is stated as novel (C136). While this is an interpretation rather than direct proof, it is well-supported by the systematic geometric data showing spiral instability in narrow chambers.

results.result: Traveling waves in large chambers result from the interaction and annihilation of multiple spiral centers combined with reflection from chamber walls. This mechanism explains the transition from spiral to traveling wave patterns as chamber area increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C145-C146, and C157 provide a mechanistic explanation for traveling wave formation that is consistent with the phase diagram data showing traveling waves in large chambers. The interpretation builds logically on the observation of spirals as the fundamental pattern. While direct visualization of spiral annihilation is not explicitly shown, the explanation is consistent with the geometric trends and previous observations on 2D surfaces.

results.result: The actual Min protein concentrations in chambers were measured using GFP calibration: MinD = 4.5 ± 0.5 μM, MinE = 6 ± 3 μM, with a MinE/MinD ratio of 1.3 ± 0.5. These concentrations were ~5-fold higher than injected stock solutions, with wide distribution particularly for MinE, and no correlation with chamber size.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 report concentration measurements from 52 chambers using a well-described GFP calibration method. The ~5-fold enrichment (C93) is explained by membrane binding during injection. The wide distribution for MinE (C94) and lack of size dependence (C95) are clearly stated. The methodology appears sound, though the large variance in MinE concentration (±3 μM, 50% CV) raises questions about experimental control that are not fully addressed.

results.result: 3D confinement reduces the Min wavelength by approximately 2-fold compared to 2D surfaces: from 78 ± 12 μm on flat SLBs to 43 ± 6 μm in confined chambers at room temperature. This demonstrates that full 3D confinement has a clear effect on the characteristic length scale of the Min system.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 and C158 report wavelength measurements with appropriate sample sizes (n=35 for chambers, n=30 for 2D surfaces) and statistical parameters. The comparison uses identical protein and lipid compositions, providing a valid controlled comparison. The 2-fold reduction is statistically significant and clearly demonstrates the effect of 3D confinement on wavelength.

results.result: The reduced wavelength in confined chambers is accompanied by reduced velocity: 0.3 ± 0.1 μm/s in chambers versus 0.6 ± 0.2 μm/s on flat SLB surfaces at room temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 report velocity measurements (n=333 chambers, n=30 flat surfaces) showing a 2-fold reduction accompanying the wavelength reduction. The measurements are consistent with previous literature values for 2D surfaces (C103). The coupled reduction in both wavelength and velocity is well-documented.

results.result: Elevated temperature (37°C) reduces Min wavelength, but the effect is much larger on 2D surfaces (78→48 μm) than in 3D confined chambers (43→37 μm). In confined chambers, geometric confinement is the major determinant of wavelength, with temperature adding only marginal further reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 report wavelength measurements at 37°C with statistical testing (t-test, p=0.001). The differential temperature effect between 2D and 3D systems is clearly documented. The interpretation that confinement dominates over temperature in 3D chambers (C173-C175) is well-supported by the data showing only a small decrease (43→37 μm) compared to the large 2D effect (78→48 μm).

results.result: Elevated temperature increases Min propagation velocity, approximately doubling from 23°C to 37°C in both 2D surfaces and 3D confinement (chambers: 0.3→0.5 μm/s; flat SLB: 0.6→1.4 μm/s). This is consistent with in vivo observations where oscillation period decreases with temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 report velocity measurements at 37°C (n=162 chambers, n=34 waves) showing approximately 2-fold increases in both systems. The comparison to in vivo behavior (C120) with citation to Touhami et al. 2006 provides validation. The observation that wavelength decreases while velocity increases (C176) demonstrates decoupling of these parameters.

results.result: Increasing medium viscosity to bacterial-level (9.9 cP using 4% PEG/Ficol/BSA) reduces wavelength by 2-fold (43→23 μm) but causes a >10-fold decrease in velocity (0.3→0.02 μm/s). Even at this high viscosity, the wavelength remains ~5-fold larger than in vivo, and further viscosity increases are unlikely to match both in vivo wavelength and velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 and C165-C169 report viscosity experiments (n=17) with well-characterized crowding solution. The wavelength reduction is comparable to previous work (C108), but the velocity decrease is much larger than observed by Martos et al., attributed to 3D vs 2D differences (C110). The conclusion that viscosity alone cannot reconcile in vitro/in vivo differences (C169) is logically sound given that velocity is already at or below in vivo levels while wavelength remains 5-fold higher (C166, C168).

results.result: Despite chamber height (2.4 μm) being close to bacterial diameter (1 μm) and using bacterial-level viscosity, the in vitro wavelength remains ~5 times larger than in vivo. Even with elevated temperature and high viscosity in 3D confined structures, in vitro Min behavior does not quantitatively reproduce in vivo behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C164, C166, and C180 consistently report the persistent ~5-fold discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo wavelengths despite multiple attempts to match in vivo conditions. This is a well-documented negative result showing that geometric confinement, temperature, and viscosity together are insufficient to fully explain in vivo behavior. The conclusion is appropriately cautious and well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data.

results.result: The geometry selection properties of the Min system at 37°C are very similar to those at room temperature: rotational patterns dominate at low aspect ratios and decrease as aspect ratio increases, oscillations occur mainly in narrow chambers, and traveling waves dominate in long/large chambers.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 report observations from 198 chambers at 37°C showing similar geometric selection rules as at room temperature. The phase diagram at 37°C (Figure 4e) shows the same three-region structure, though with more scatter noted. This demonstrates robustness of geometric selection rules across temperatures.

results.result: In contrast to in vivo behavior where wavelength is temperature-independent, the in vitro wavelength is temperature-dependent. Since bulk viscosity changes only 1.3-fold from 23°C to 37°C, the temperature effect must be attributed to changes in reaction parameters, most likely ATP hydrolysis rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 and C172 identify a key difference between in vivo and in vitro systems with appropriate citation to in vivo work (C20). The reasoning that excludes diffusion changes (1.3-fold viscosity change, C122) and implicates reaction parameters is sound. The suggestion of ATP hydrolysis rate (C172) is speculative but reasonable. This represents a valid mechanistic insight.

results.result: The dynamical characteristics of the Min system (wavelength and velocity) are decoupled parameters that can be tuned in opposite directions through at least three different mechanisms: confinement, temperature, and bulk viscosity.
results.evaluation: Claims C124, C177, and C179 synthesize observations showing that wavelength and velocity respond differently to various perturbations (e.g., temperature increases velocity while decreasing wavelength; viscosity decreases both but at different rates). This conclusion is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data across multiple conditions.

results.result: Total confinement of the Min system in 3D chambers leads to three main pattern types: rotational spiral waves (majority), periodic oscillations (mainly in narrow chambers), and traveling waves (mainly when one dimension exceeds the typical spatial length scale). Both oscillations and traveling waves result from interrelation between the spiral symmetry-breaking mechanism and confinement effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C125, C186, and C188 provide a comprehensive summary of the main findings. The three pattern types are well-documented throughout the manuscript. The mechanistic interpretation (C188) that oscillations and waves derive from spiral patterns interacting with confinement is supported by the phase diagram data and geometric analysis, though it remains an interpretation rather than direct proof.

results.result: In vitro Min patterns may emanate from a different symmetry-breaking mechanism than in vivo oscillations. The abundance of spirals in vitro versus their absence in vivo, and the different character of oscillations (in vitro: traveling wave-like; in vivo: polar zone replacement), suggest mechanistic differences despite using the same proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 and C137-C142 present speculative interpretations about different symmetry-breaking mechanisms. While the observations are valid (spirals absent in vivo per C137, different oscillation character per C139-C141), the conclusion of fundamentally different mechanisms is not definitively proven. Alternative explanations (e.g., additional cellular factors, different parameter regimes of the same mechanism) are not fully excluded. This remains an interesting hypothesis requiring further validation.

results.result: In vivo traveling waves represent abnormal behavior (MinE impairment or anomalous conditions), while in vitro they are a generic feature. The high protein concentration and high surface-to-volume ratio in vitro (compared to in vivo where cytosolic concentration drops during pattern formation) may explain this difference. Multiple factors determine in vitro pattern formation: surface-to-volume ratio, protein concentration, confinement, and MinE membrane binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C155 synthesize observations about traveling waves and protein concentrations to propose a mechanistic explanation. The distinction between in vivo (abnormal) and in vitro (generic) traveling waves is well-documented (C143-C144). The concentration measurements (C147, C93-C98) support the high-concentration hypothesis. The integration with recent work by Vecchiarelli et al. (C149-C151) provides external validation. The multi-factorial conclusion (C152) is appropriately nuanced.

results.result: The wavelength reduction in 3D chambers may result from two mechanisms: lateral confinement selecting smaller-wavelength modes, and/or height reduction changing the balance between free and membrane-bound Min proteins. Theoretical predictions support that reducing protein volume above the surface drives wavelength to lower values.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C163 propose two plausible mechanisms for wavelength reduction, supported by theoretical predictions from Halatek and Frey (personal communication, C161) and published work by Thalmeier et al. (C162). While these are mechanistic hypotheses rather than proven mechanisms, they are well-grounded in reaction-diffusion theory and supported by the observation that both wavelength and velocity decrease with height reduction (C163).

results.result: Additional dynamical parameters beyond confinement, temperature, and viscosity are probably necessary to reproduce in vivo behavior. Possibilities include changes in Min protein concentration, reaction rates, or yet unidentified protein species that affect membrane organization or Min protein interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C178 and C181-C185 acknowledge the limitations of the current study and propose future directions. The conclusion that additional parameters are needed (C181) is well-supported by the persistent in vitro/in vivo discrepancy (C180). The suggestions are appropriately speculative, citing evidence for Min effects on membrane organization (C183) and protein interactions (C184). This represents honest assessment of what remains unexplained.

results.result: Spiral waves are common in various biological and chemical reaction-diffusion processes (Dictyostelium, Xenopus oocytes, Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction) and were previously observed for Min on flat SLBs. In nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, multiple symmetry-breaking mechanisms can coexist in different parameter regimes.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 provide appropriate context from the literature on spiral waves in reaction-diffusion systems. The citations to established work (Epstein and Pojman 1998, Loose et al. 2008, Hagan 1982, Yang et al. 2002) support these background statements. This contextualizes the Min spiral observations within broader pattern formation theory.

results.result: Theoretical work by Bonny et al. showed traveling waves could be produced by increasing Min concentration by 63% or increasing MinE/MinD ratio. In chambers with high surface-to-volume ratio and high Min concentration, the cumulative effect of spiral annihilation and wall reflection can produce traveling waves.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157 connect the experimental observations to theoretical predictions. The citation to Bonny et al. 2013 (C156) supports that concentration increases can produce traveling waves theoretically. The mechanistic explanation for traveling wave formation (C157) integrates the geometric analysis with concentration measurements, providing a coherent framework.

results.result: Comprehensive literature review establishing: Min system biology and biochemistry (proteins, interactions, in vivo behavior in various cell geometries), previous in vitro reconstitution studies (2D SLBs, semi-confined chambers, effects of diffusion/reaction parameters), theoretical modeling efforts and their limitations, and the gap in knowledge regarding fully confined 3D geometries.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C62 provide extensive background with appropriate citations throughout. The review accurately represents prior work on Min biology (C7-C29), in vitro reconstitution (C30-C49), and theoretical modeling (C50-C58). The identification of knowledge gaps (C59-C62) appropriately motivates the current study. This is a thorough and well-cited literature review.
